name: Arolsen Archives
description: Thirty million documents on Nazi persecution: camp registration cards, transport and transfer lists, labour deployment, death books, displaced-persons and postwar tracing files.
tip: Search the town as well as the person. A village name returns the neighbours, and the neighbours' records will place your family.

name: Yad Vashem, Central Database of Shoah Victims' Names
description: Pages of Testimony, filled in by surviving relatives, so they carry parents, spouses, ages and hometowns that no camp form records.
tip: Read the submitter. A Page filed by a relative is a living-family lead, and the address and date on it are where to start looking for descendants.

name: USHMM Collections
description: Holds RG-31.136, the full digitisation of the Subcarpathian regional archive, roughly 488,000 images of the civil registers, browsable by fund, opus and file.
tip: Use JewishGen to find the fund and file number first, then come here to read the actual page.

name: JewishGen
description: Indexed vital records for Subcarpathia, Máramaros, Hungary, Galicia and much of eastern Europe, plus the 1921 Czechoslovak census and the burial registry.
tip: Search surname plus town, never a given name first. Given names collide across languages; a village does not.

name: Sub-Carpathia Genealogy
description: The transcription project behind the JewishGen Subcarpathia records, run by Roberta Solit. Also holds more than 25,000 tombstone photographs that are not on JewishGen.
tip: Buy the scan when you need the image, but check first whether the index alone answers your question. It often does.

name: Gesher Galicia
description: The All-Galicia Database, for anywhere that was Austrian Galicia: today's south-eastern Poland and western Ukraine.
tip: Search by locality when a surname returns nothing. Many towns are indexed by place but not by name.

name: JRI-Poland
description: Jewish records indexing for Poland, and the natural companion to Gesher Galicia for anything on the Polish side of the border.

name: Hungaricana
description: Hungarian and Czechoslovak archival collections, including the 1921 census sheets that put a whole household on one page: everyone under one roof, with ages and birthplaces.
tip: A census sheet is the fastest way to prove two people were family, because it shows them living together.

name: Terezín Memorial database
description: Prisoner and transport cards for Terezín, including people who arrived on the last evacuation transports in spring 1945 and were liberated there.

name: Gross-Rosen Museum database
description: Prisoner records for Gross-Rosen and its very large network of subcamps, which absorbed many Hungarian Jews in 1944.

name: JewishGen KehilaLinks
description: Volunteer-built town pages. For this region they carry Marshall Katz's photographs and transcriptions of about a hundred Subcarpathian cemeteries.
tip: A gravestone names the father. When the civil registers run out, a stone can give you the next generation up.

name: JOWBR, the burial registry
description: Indexed burials worldwide, searchable by name, with plot positions and often the father's name from the inscription.

name: USC Shoah Foundation Visual History Archive
description: More than fifty thousand recorded survivor testimonies, indexed by person, place and topic, so you can find someone who was in the same village or on the same transport.
tip: Search the town. A neighbour's testimony often describes your family by name.

name: Centropa
description: Long interviews with central European Jewish families, published with their own photographs and captions naming everyone in the frame.

name: DEGOB protocols
description: Roughly five thousand statements taken from Hungarian survivors in 1945, within months of liberation, and the Kassa log of deportation trains.

name: Genealogy Indexer
description: Full-text search across digitised business directories, yizkor books, school and military lists from central and eastern Europe.
tip: This is where you establish a negative. Finding that a family is absent from three editions of a directory is evidence about how they lived.

name: Yizkor books
description: Memorial books written by a town's own survivors after the war. They give the roundup date, the route, the names of the rabbi and the shochet, and how many households there were.
tip: Many are also scanned in full on archive.org even when the translation on JewishGen is partial.
